name: East Face
approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake roughly 2 more miles to the Pacific Crest Trail junction near Escondido Ridge and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path fords back to creek-left after about 200 yards, crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. A rock buttress called Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft), overlooking Chimney Creek's waterfalls, marks the top of the brush; most parties reach it in 4-5 hours from the trailhead. From Sunrise Knob, climb the moraine crest to roughly 5,400 ft and a boulder-strewn basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier — a large boulder near the creek has 3+ established bivy sites and is the standard high camp (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip). Reliable water is at Pete Lake and the low Chimney Creek crossings; above the moraine plan on melting snow or glacier water. Hazards: the avalanche-path crossing (blowdown, lingering snow/avalanche debris into early summer), loose/brushy ravine crossings, and standard glacier travel hazards (crevasses, moats) gaining and crossing the Chimney Glacier to the base of the route.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Trailhead elevations are given from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further. Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half. The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and parties consistently describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest between the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. One party puts its start at an obvious logjam giving creek access, only about twenty yards inside the forest rather than the two hundred sometimes given. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on. One known wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues left through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth. The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. A rock buttress above the waterfalls is known as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and planning three days is a common recommendation for what many parties attempt in two.
approach_variants.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bivy the thing to identify is the U-Gap, the notch that almost every party climbing this peak passes through. Chimney Rock is the second peak to the right of the U-Gap. Fix that relationship from camp, in daylight, before you are on the glacier. Getting onto the upper glacier is a three-way choice and it is always the same three: a rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall (the usual, described as grungy and wet), a snow finger far to the left, or the icefall climbed directly if you have screws and the conditions for it. The moat is the arrival, and whether you can get from snow onto rock at all is the crux of the day rather than a formality. Parties describe reaching the bergschrund at the foot of the face and finding it large, then getting across only because fallen ice blocks had tumbled in and built a ramp and platform to step off. If there is no such ramp there may be no way onto the rock, and that is a condition of the season, not a route-finding failure. Above the U-Gap the traverse across the South Peak toward the Main Peak is a sequence of ledges that one party fairly called improbable — the first of them begins about fifteen vertical feet below the U-Gap on its east side, so a search at gap level finds nothing. Negative marker worth carrying: the blind chimney on the way to the broad ledge under the summit tower was found by one party to be a very loose, dangerous, grungy gully. They backed out of it and instead downclimbed about fifty feet from the Main Notch and picked up an obvious reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp leading to the small notch they wanted. If you are grovelling in rotten grunge you are probably in the feature they abandoned. A final sanity check on how rarely this is done: the summit register suggests roughly one party a year. Do not expect a boot track or fresh tat to confirm anything for you.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 80, go north on Bullfrog Road through two traffic circles onto SR 903, then follow SR 903 through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake to Cooper Lake Road (FR 46), about 16.8 miles from the freeway. Turn left on FR 46 for 4.7 miles, then right on FR 4616 for about 1 mile to the Pete Lake trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, plus a free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.
waypoints.directions: Follow Pete Lake Trail #1323 up the Cooper River valley, about 4.5 nearly flat forested miles, to the lake.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the trail beyond the lake to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near Lemah Meadow.

waypoints.name: Avalanche path at Chimney Creek confluence
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT at the first switchback in this avalanche path; a faint, sometimes flagged climber's path drops to a log crossing of the creek and is easy to lose in fog or low light.
waypoints.directions: Turn north on the PCT, not toward Spectacle Lake, and follow it roughly a mile to where it crosses a wide old avalanche path with heavy blowdown near Chimney Creek and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that first switchback and look west for twin waterfalls spilling out of the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Standard 2-3 day basecamp on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls, roughly 6 hours' hike from the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Leave the PCT at the switchback on a faint climbers' path, marked only intermittently with flagging and cairns, that climbs the forest right of the falls between two rounded rock outcrops and a cliff band. Do not follow it up a rocky gully; the line continues left through vine maple and alder, crosses three brushy ravines, and breaks out at Sunrise Knob, the rock buttress above the falls.

waypoints.name: Chimney Glacier bergschrund/moat
waypoints.note: A short pitch of hard ~45-degree glacier ice and a bergschrund/moat crossing guard the base of the East Face; crampons and axe required, and the moat widens as the season progresses.
waypoints.directions: From camp, make your way onto the lower Chimney Glacier and rope up. Cross it and break through the cliff band onto the upper glacier, usually by the rock-and-snow gully just left of the icefall (a snow finger far to the left and the icefall itself are the alternatives), then cross the upper glacier to the foot of the gully that leads to the U-Gap, where the moat separates ice from rock.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, Main (Central) Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, topped out via 3 pitches of 5.3 rock above the moat; descend via rappels and 3rd-class downclimbing back to the glacier.
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat where conditions allow and climb the loose gully toward the U-Gap. About 15 ft below the gap, leave it on the east side onto exposed ledges that wrap around the South Peak to the Main Notch, drop about 50 ft and take a reddish ramp up to the Key Ledge below the summit tower, then climb three pitches of class 4 and low fifth class, the last a chimney that tops out a few feet from the summit cairn.

descent_text: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two rappels on a single rope; some parties make three), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Note: some parties, especially those who climbed a more direct line up the face, instead reverse the entire face with a longer string of rappels — trip reports for the harder Direct East Face variant describe as many as five to six rappels straight down the glacier-facing slabs with good anchors reported the whole way down — but the descent via the saddle/gully is the more commonly reported line for the standard East Face route. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
